rmt-2015-power-01a.title: Check each table
rmt-2015-power-01a.body:
Proportional means each player gets at least $\frac12$.

(i) Player 2 values only $A$, so Player 2 must get $A$. Then Player 1 gets $\{B,C\}$, worth $0.3+0.3=0.6\ge\frac12$. Division: 1: $\{B,C\}$, 2: $\{A\}$.

(ii) Player 1 needs $A$ (without $A$ they have at most $0.4$), and Player 2 needs $A$ too (without $A$, at most $0.4$). Both cannot receive $A$, so there is no proportional division.

(iii) The values are identical for both players: $A=0.3$, $B=0.5$, $C=0.2$. Give $B$ to one player ($0.5$) and $\{A,C\}$ to the other ($0.3+0.2=0.5$): 1: $\{A,C\}$, 2: $\{B\}$.

rmt-2015-power-01b.title: Equal shares
rmt-2015-power-01b.body: Give each of the $n$ players the fraction $\frac1n$ of every good. By linearity, player $i$ receives total value $\frac1n\sum_{g\in G}v_i(g)=\frac1n v_i(G)=\frac1n$. So every player receives exactly $\frac1n$, and the division is proportional. ∎

rmt-2015-power-01c.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-01c.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose all players have the same value function $v$ and let player $i$ receive fraction $x_{ig}$ of good $g$ (so $\sum_ix_{ig}=1$). The total value received by all players is $\sum_i\sum_g x_{ig}v(g)=\sum_gv(g)=1$. If every player received more than $\frac1n$, the sum would exceed $1$, a contradiction. So no super proportional division exists.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose not all value functions coincide ($n\ge2$). Start from the equal split in which each player has $\frac1n$ of every good, worth exactly $\frac1n$ to everyone.

*Claim.* If $v_i\ne v_j$, there are goods $g,h$ with $v_i(g)v_j(h)>v_j(g)v_i(h)$. Indeed, if all the cross products $v_i(g)v_j(h)-v_j(g)v_i(h)$ vanished then the vectors $(v_i(g))_g$ and $(v_j(g))_g$ would be proportional; since both sum to $1$ they would be equal. So some cross product is nonzero; swap names of $g,h$ if necessary to make it positive.

With such $g,h$ we have $v_i(g)>0$ and $v_j(h)>0$ and $\frac{v_i(h)}{v_i(g)}<\frac{v_j(h)}{v_j(g)}$ (the right side is $+\infty$ if $v_j(g)=0$). Pick $r$ strictly between. Let player $i$ give an amount $\varepsilon$ of $h$ to $j$ and receive an amount $\delta=r\varepsilon$ of $g$ from $j$. Then $i$ gains $\delta v_i(g)-\varepsilon v_i(h)=\varepsilon\big(rv_i(g)-v_i(h)\big)>0$ and $j$ gains $\varepsilon v_j(h)-\delta v_j(g)=\varepsilon\big(v_j(h)-rv_j(g)\big)>0$. Both strictly gain.

Now, since not all functions agree, every player $i$ has a partner $p(i)$ with $v_{p(i)}\ne v_i$ (otherwise everyone would equal $v_i$). For each $i$ perform such a trade $T_i$ between $i$ and $p(i)$, with all amounts $\varepsilon$ so tiny that the total amount taken from any player's holding of any good is less than $\frac1n$ (at most $2n$ trades touch a given player). Values are additive, so each player's total value is $\frac1n$ plus the sum of the gains from the trades they take part in; each such gain is strictly positive and every player takes part in at least one trade ($T_i$). Hence everybody gets strictly more than $\frac1n$. ∎

rmt-2015-power-02a.title: Part (i)
rmt-2015-power-02a.body:
Give Player 1 $\{C,D\}$, Player 2 $\{B\}$, Player 3 $\{A\}$.
- Player 1 receives $0.5$; sees $\{B\}$ and $\{A\}$ as $0.25$ each.
- Player 2 receives $0.4$; sees $\{A\}=0.3$ and $\{C,D\}=0.3$.
- Player 3 receives $0.5$ (good $A$); sees $\{B\}=0$ and $\{C,D\}=0.5$.

Nobody prefers another bundle, so the division is envy-free.

rmt-2015-power-02a.title: Part (ii)
rmt-2015-power-02a.body: Everybody values every good positively, so anyone who gets nothing envies someone; hence the bundles have sizes $2,1,1$ in some order. Player 1 values every good at $0.25$, so a player holding one good envies a player holding two; thus Player 1 must be the one with two goods (if Player 1 held one good, the other two players could hold at most one each, only $3$ goods in total). Now Player 2 holds a single good, worth at most $0.3$, while Player 1's pair is worth at least $0.2+0.2=0.4$ to Player 2. So Player 2 is envious. Hence no envy-free division exists.

rmt-2015-power-02b.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-02b.body: Suppose an envy-free division gives player $i$ total value $v_i(G_i)<\frac1n$. The other $n-1$ bundles together are worth $1-v_i(G_i)>\frac{n-1}n$ to player $i$ (the bundles partition $G$), so one of them, $G_j$, has $v_i(G_j)>\frac{1}{n-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}n=\frac1n>v_i(G_i)$. Then player $i$ envies $j$, contradiction. So everyone receives at least $\frac1n$. ∎

rmt-2015-power-02c.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-02c.body: Let the division be proportional with two players. Player $i$ receives $v_i(G_i)\ge\frac12$, and the other bundle is the rest of $G$, so $v_i(G_j)=1-v_i(G_i)\le\frac12\le v_i(G_i)$. Hence no one envies the other. ∎

rmt-2015-power-02d.title: Counterexample
rmt-2015-power-02d.body:
Three players, indivisible goods $A,B,C$ with
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ \hline A & 0.4 & 0.6 & 0 \\ B & 0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \\ C & 0.6 & 0 & 0.4\end{array}$$
Give $A$ to Player 1, $B$ to Player 2, $C$ to Player 3. Player 1 gets $0.4$, Player 2 gets $0.4$, Player 3 gets $0.4$: all more than $\frac13$, so the division is proportional. But Player 1 values Player 3's good $C$ at $0.6>0.4$, so Player 1 envies Player 3. Hence proportional does not imply envy-free for three players.

rmt-2015-power-03a.title: Enumerate the 16 divisions
rmt-2015-power-03a.body:
For each set $S$ given to Player 1 (the rest to Player 2), the pair (value to 1, value to 2) is:

$\varnothing$: $(0,1)$; $A$: $(0.3,0.9)$; $B$: $(0.3,0.8)$; $C$: $(0.2,0.7)$; $D$: $(0.2,0.6)$; $AB$: $(0.6,0.7)$; $AC$: $(0.5,0.6)$; $AD$: $(0.5,0.5)$; $BC$: $(0.5,0.5)$; $BD$: $(0.5,0.4)$; $CD$: $(0.4,0.3)$; $ABC$: $(0.8,0.4)$; $ABD$: $(0.8,0.3)$; $ACD$: $(0.7,0.2)$; $BCD$: $(0.7,0.1)$; $ABCD$: $(1,0)$.

The non-dominated pairs are $(0,1)$, $(0.3,0.9)$, $(0.6,0.7)$, $(0.8,0.4)$, $(1,0)$; every other pair is dominated by one of these (for instance $(0.3,0.8)\le(0.3,0.9)$, $(0.5,0.6)\le(0.6,0.7)$, $(0.8,0.3)\le(0.8,0.4)$, $(0.7,0.2)\le(0.8,0.4)$).

So the Pareto efficient divisions are: 1 gets everything; 1 gets $\{A,B,C\}$ and 2 gets $\{D\}$; 1 gets $\{A,B\}$ and 2 gets $\{C,D\}$; 1 gets $\{A\}$ and 2 gets $\{B,C,D\}$; 2 gets everything.

Proportional means both values are at least $0.5$: only $(0.6,0.7)$, i.e. 1: $\{A,B\}$, 2: $\{C,D\}$.

rmt-2015-power-03b.title: Example
rmt-2015-power-03b.body:
Take
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.5 & 0 \\ B & 0 & 0.5 \\ C & 0.5 & 0.5\end{array}$$
The division 1: $\{A,B\}$, 2: $\{C\}$ gives Player 1 value $0.5$ and Player 2 value $0.5$, so it is proportional. But 1: $\{A,C\}$, 2: $\{B\}$ gives Player 1 value $1$ and Player 2 value $0.5$: nobody is worse off and Player 1 is strictly better off, so the first division is not Pareto efficient.

rmt-2015-power-03c.title: Counterexample
rmt-2015-power-03c.body:
The "if" direction is true (a dominating trade shows the division is not Pareto efficient), but the "only if" direction fails with three players. Take
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ \hline A & 0.4 & 0.6 & 0 \\ B & 0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \\ C & 0.6 & 0 & 0.4\end{array}$$
and the division 1: $A$, 2: $B$, 3: $C$ (each gets $0.4$). The cyclic division 1: $C$, 2: $A$, 3: $B$ gives each player $0.6$, so it dominates; hence the division is not Pareto efficient.

But no trade between two players helps: Player 1 holds $A$ and Player 2 holds $B$, and Player 1 values $B$ at $0$, so any trade of part of $A$ for part of $B$ makes Player 1 strictly worse off; Player 2 holds $B$ and Player 3 holds $C$, and Player 2 values $C$ at $0$ (strictly worse off); Player 3 holds $C$ and Player 1 holds $A$, and Player 3 values $A$ at $0$ (strictly worse off). So no trade between two players yields a dominating division, and the statement is false.

rmt-2015-power-04a.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-04a.body:
After the trade Player 1's value changes by $t\,v_1(g_j)-s\,v_1(g_i)$ and Player 2's by $s\,v_2(g_i)-t\,v_2(g_j)$.

If Player 1 gains, $t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)$, hence $t\,v_2(g_j)\ge t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)\ge s\,v_2(g_i)$, so Player 2's change is negative.

If Player 2 gains, $s\,v_2(g_i)>t\,v_2(g_j)$, hence $s\,v_1(g_i)\ge s\,v_2(g_i)>t\,v_2(g_j)\ge t\,v_1(g_j)$, so Player 1's change is negative. ∎

rmt-2015-power-04b.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-04b.body:
Rearranging the hypothesis gives $\dfrac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}\le\dfrac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}$.

If Player 1 gains, $t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)$, so $\dfrac st<\dfrac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}\le\dfrac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}$, i.e. $s\,v_2(g_i)<t\,v_2(g_j)$: Player 2 loses.

If Player 2 gains, $s\,v_2(g_i)>t\,v_2(g_j)$, so $\dfrac st>\dfrac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}\ge\dfrac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}$, i.e. $s\,v_1(g_i)>t\,v_1(g_j)$: Player 1 loses. ∎

rmt-2015-power-04c.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-04c.body:
*Termination.* At the start Player 1 has value $W_1\ge W_2$, Player 2's value. As Player 1 hands over $g_{i_r}$, then $g_{i_{r-1}}$, ..., continuously, Player 1's value decreases continuously and Player 2's increases continuously. If everything were handed over, Player 1 would have value $0$ and Player 2 value $1$. So the difference (Player 1's value minus Player 2's) is continuous, is $\ge0$ at the start and is $-1<0$ at the end. By the intermediate value theorem it is $0$ at some point (reached after finitely many goods are touched), and the procedure stops there with both players having the same value $x$.

*Pareto efficiency.* Because of the order of transfers, the final division has the following shape: for some ratio $\theta\ge1$, Player 1 holds all of every good with ratio $\frac{v_1}{v_2}>\theta$, Player 2 holds all of every good with ratio $<\theta$, and goods with ratio exactly $\theta$ may be split. (If the process stops exactly at the boundary where all remaining goods of Player 1 have $v_2=0$, any $\theta\ge1$ at least as large as the largest finite ratio works.) Let $p_g$ be the fraction of $g$ held by Player 1. For any division with fractions $p'_g$,
$$v_1+\theta v_2=\sum_g\Big(p'_g\,v_1(g)+\theta(1-p'_g)v_2(g)\Big)=\theta+\sum_gp'_g\big(v_1(g)-\theta v_2(g)\big),$$
which is largest when $p'_g=1$ if $v_1(g)>\theta v_2(g)$ and $p'_g=0$ if $v_1(g)<\theta v_2(g)$. The final division has exactly this form, so it maximizes $v_1+\theta v_2$ over all divisions. If some division dominated it, then $v_1'\ge x$, $v_2'\ge x$ with one inequality strict, so $v'_1+\theta v_2'>x+\theta x$, contradicting maximality (as $\theta>0$). So it is Pareto efficient. (Equivalently, any further trade that helps one player must hurt the other, by 4(a) and 4(b).)

*Envy-freeness.* Both players end with value $x$, so each values the other's bundle at $1-x$. If $x<\frac12$, swapping the two bundles would give each player $1-x>x$, a division dominating the final one, contradicting Pareto efficiency. Hence $x\ge\frac12\ge1-x$ and neither player envies the other. ∎

rmt-2015-power-05a.title: Check each
rmt-2015-power-05a.body:
The divider's two bundles must each be worth exactly $\frac12$ to the divider, and the chooser must take a bundle that is at least as good for her.

(i) Player 1 as divider: $S$ is worth $0.5$ and $\{C,V\}$ is worth $0.2+0.3=0.5$ to Player 1. Player 2 values $\{C,V\}$ at $0.7>0.3$, so she picks $\{C,V\}$ and Player 1 keeps $S$. **Possible; Player 1 was the divider.**

(ii) If Player 1 divided into $\{C,V\}$ and $\{S\}$, Player 2 would choose $\{C,V\}$ (worth $0.7$), leaving Player 1 with $S$, not this outcome. If Player 2 divided, the bundles must be worth $\frac12$ to her, but $\{C,V\}=0.7$ and $\{S\}=0.3$. **Not possible.**

(iii) Player 1 would get $0.3+0.25=0.55\ne\frac12$ and Player 2 would get $0.3+0.15=0.45\ne\frac12$. Whoever the divider is, their own bundle must be worth exactly $\frac12$ to them. **Not possible.**

(iv) Player 2's bundle $\{C,\frac12V\}$ is worth $0.3+0.2=0.5$ to her and so is $\{\frac12V,S\}$ ($0.2+0.3$), so Player 2 can be the divider. Player 1 values $\{\frac12V,S\}$ at $0.15+0.5=0.65>0.35$, so Player 1 chooses it. **Possible; Player 2 was the divider.**

rmt-2015-power-05b.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-05b.body: The divider values both sets at $\frac12$, so the divider is content with whichever set remains and does not envy the chooser. The chooser picks the set she values at least as much as the other, so she does not envy the divider. Hence the division is envy-free. ∎

rmt-2015-power-05c.title: Counterexample
rmt-2015-power-05c.body:
Let $G=\{C,V\}$ with
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline C & 1 & 0 \\ V & 0 & 1\end{array}$$Player 1 may divide $G$ into two bundles each consisting of half of $C$ and half of $V$; each is worth $\frac12$ to Player 1. Player 2 also values each at $\frac12$ and takes either one. Both players receive $\frac12$. But giving $C$ to Player 1 and $V$ to Player 2 gives each of them value $1$, which dominates. So the outcome of Divide and Choose need not be Pareto efficient.

rmt-2015-power-05d.title: Counterexample
rmt-2015-power-05d.body: Let $G=\{A,B,C\}$ with $v_1=(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13)$, $v_2=(0.5,0.25,0.25)$ and $v_3=(0.8,0.1,0.1)$ on $(A,B,C)$. Player 1 may divide $G$ into the three sets $\{A\},\{B\},\{C\}$ (each worth $\frac13$ to him). Player 2 chooses $\{A\}$ (her favorite). Player 3 must choose between $\{B\}$ and $\{C\}$ and gets only $0.1$, but values Player 2's set $\{A\}$ at $0.8$. So Player 3 envies Player 2 and the procedure is not envy-free.

rmt-2015-power-06a.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-06a.body: Each player's value of the left piece is a continuous nondecreasing function of the knife position, going from $0$ to $1$, so some player reaches $\frac12$ and the procedure stops (the first time any player does). Suppose Player $A$ stops it at position $x$. Then $A$ values the left piece at exactly $\frac12$ and so the right piece at exactly $\frac12$; $A$ is content with the left piece. The other player $B$ did not call stop earlier, so at all positions before $x$ and, by continuity, at $x$ itself $B$ values the left piece at most $\frac12$. Hence $B$ values the right piece at least $\frac12$, at least as much as the left piece, and $B$ does not envy $A$. (If both reach $\frac12$ simultaneously, both are indifferent.) ∎

rmt-2015-power-06b.title: Induction on n
rmt-2015-power-06b.body:
We prove: for any $n$ players and any (sub)cake, each player ends up with at least $\frac1n$ of the value she assigns to that cake. For $n=1$ the single player takes everything.

Assume it holds for $n-1$ players. In the first round some player stops the knife at the first moment any player reaches $\frac1n$ of her value of the whole; she receives exactly $\frac1n$ of her value. Every other player $j$ has not yet reached $\frac1n$, so (by continuity, at the stopping point) values the left piece at most $\frac1n$ of the whole; hence she values the remainder at least $1-\frac1n=\frac{n-1}n$ of the whole. By the induction hypothesis applied to the remainder with $n-1$ players, she finally receives at least $\frac1{n-1}$ of her value of the remainder, which is at least $\frac1{n-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}n=\frac1n$ of her value of the whole. So all $n$ players get at least $\frac1n$. ∎

rmt-2015-power-06c.title: Proof
rmt-2015-power-06c.body:
(i) Let $g(t)$ be Player 2's value of the center piece at time $t$; it is continuous since the knives move continuously. At the start the center piece is $[0,m]$, with $g(0)=g_0$. The sweep ends with the right knife at $1$ and the center piece $[a^*,1]$, where Player 1 values $[a^*,1]$ at $\frac12$; since Player 1's density is positive, $a^*=m$, so the final center piece is $[m,1]$, with Player 2's value $1-g_0$. If $g_0=\frac12$ she stops immediately. Otherwise $g_0-\frac12$ and $(1-g_0)-\frac12$ have opposite signs, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a time $t'$ with $g(t')=\frac12$, and Player 2 stops the procedure then. (Player 2 is not required to stop earlier, so the procedure stops at the first such $t'$.)

(ii) When the procedure stops, the center piece is worth exactly $\frac12$ to Player 1 (by the construction) and exactly $\frac12$ to Player 2 (by her stopping condition). The rest of the cake is therefore also worth $1-\frac12=\frac12$ to each of them. So each player values both pieces at exactly $\frac12$: the division is exact. In particular nobody values the other's piece more than their own (envy-free) and everyone gets at least $\frac12$ (proportional). ∎

rmt-2015-power-07a.title: Maximize against Player 2's choice
rmt-2015-power-07a.body:
Player 1 wants to end with a bundle $S$ that Player 2 does not choose, i.e. worth strictly less than $\frac12$ to Player 2 (so the other bundle is strictly better for her), while maximizing the value of $S$ to Player 1. This is a fractional knapsack: value to Player 1 per unit of Player 2's value is $\frac{0.5}{0.3}$ for $C$, $\frac{0.3}{0.4}$ for $B$, and $\frac{0.2}{0.3}$ for $A$. So Player 1 should take all of $C$ (cost $0.3$ in Player 2's value) and then as much of $B$ as possible: a fraction $\beta$ of $B$ costs $0.4\beta$, and the budget is just under $0.2$, so $\beta<\frac12$. For any $\epsilon>0$ he can split $G$ into $\{C,(\frac12-\epsilon)B\}$ and $\{A,(\frac12+\epsilon)B\}$: Player 2 values these at $0.5-0.4\epsilon$ and $0.5+0.4\epsilon$ and takes the second, leaving Player 1 the first, worth $0.5+0.3(\frac12-\epsilon)=0.65-0.3\epsilon$ to him.

The supremum $0.65$ is not attained, so the largest value $\frac{x}{1000}$ he can guarantee has $x=649$ (any $\epsilon\le\frac1{300}$ gives at least $0.649$, and $0.65-0.3\epsilon<0.65$ always, so $0.650$ cannot be guaranteed).

**Answer: 649**

rmt-2015-power-07b.title: Lie to win B and C
rmt-2015-power-07b.body:
The third party gives each good to the player who reports the higher value (ties may be split). Player 2 reports truthfully: $A=0.3$, $B=0.4$, $C=0.3$. Player 1's report must also sum to $1$, so he can win a set of goods only if his reports on them exceed Player 2's: to win $B$ and $C$ he reports more than $0.4$ and more than $0.3$ for them (e.g. $B=0.405$, $C=0.305$, $A=0.29$), which is possible since $0.405+0.305<1$. Winning all three goods would require reports exceeding $0.3+0.4+0.3=1$, which is impossible, and winning $A$ and $B$ or $A$ and $C$ is worth less to him. Winning $B$ and $C$ gives him true value $0.3+0.5=0.8$, the best possible.

**Answer: 0.8**
